title: The Sea Sonnets 5
text:
How the sea moves, how it shines;

how it chains together greens and blues;

how it establishes, in the Caribbean zone,

its beautiful and resonant dictatorship!


How, in the transparent and pure vein

of the waters, it heaps up its gleams;

how, in its swells, it crowns itself

with light, lifting its smoothness into the air!


How it brings to its surface the deep,

the live and clear impulse of its bottom,

the strong boiling of its piercing ardor!


How, in its bonds with myth,

it is, in its eternity and in its infinity,

like God and the lines of his sky!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sonnet's exclamatory praise of the Caribbean sea as force, myth, and divinity.

title: The Sea Sonnets 4
text:
Mysterious and fugitive beauty;

beauty that is beauty in the instant.

Celestial insinuation in the wandering

mystery. Blue and rose in living water.


In lucid presence, in dazzling

and sudden appearance, elusive flame,

displayed on the face of the one who enlivens it

for the contemplator, for the lover.


In its three planes, transitory flight.

Dawns and rainbows in the sky.

On the earth, the waters and the flowers.


And in the sea? In the sea, greater wealth:

in green-blue waves, the beauty

that passes, with a burden of refinements.
editorial_note: The translation treats an apparent 'pianos' as 'planes' and keeps beauty as instant, fugitive appearance.

title: Definition
text:
The forehead, the eye, the neck and the hair.
The hair exudes glittering golds.
In naked light the neck lays itself bare.
In naked light the neck lays itself bare.


I do not know what graces its grace knots
in the chosen face, for there is no seal
that is not of grace in all that is beautiful
in beauty without possible change.


There is no change in beauty. The gaze
—clarity of the eye—, in deep and wakeful
sweetness, girds worlds of purity.


There is no change in beauty. Consistent
with its many virtues. Eye and forehead,
hair and neck in perennial beauty.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the repeated neck line and the poem's insistence on beauty without change.

title: The Sea Sonnets 3
text:
Sea of God, sea veiled and protected

by the grace of love in beauty...

I join my smallness to its greatness

and find in its fullness new meaning.


Sea of God, sea in light, sea possessed

by the mystery of the world. Its purity

—that of the fish and the ship in light and height—

moves me to thought and sound.


I do not cast anchor. The voyage is perennial.

Foam embroiders flowers on the ship's side.

I deepen into the ringleted blue.


God waits for me in the sea. And God calls me.

Perhaps He will shroud me with the branch

of the coral of his blood in its blue depth.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the sonnet's sea-voyage as a religious calling without anchorage.

title: Creation
text:
When the Lord, his hand fatigued

from shaping figures in clay,

wanted to form him, he noticed that the clay

was very little, prepared what there was

to mold him, and meditated a moment:


"With the little clay I will make him lean,

but I will press him with energy;

I will make him slender, resistant, like

a steel rod."


He carried out the work;

and afterward crowning it with grace

to make up for the absence

of robustness, he transmitted to him a spirit

among the best, and was joyful:

for lack of the athlete's strength,

he endowed him with the marvelous power

of immortality: He made him a poet!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the creation fable in which physical slightness is exchanged for poetic immortality.
